extracted.intended_audience: employers, immigration attorneys, labor certification practitioners, and stakeholders in H-1B/PERM/EB visa programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for determining and calibrating prevailing wage levels used in H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, EB-2, EB-3, and PERM programs, including data sources, occupational qualification alignment, and adjustments to wage-tier methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of "specialty occupation"
rubrics_metrics.description: The INA defines “specialty occupation” as an occupation that requires theoretical and practical application of a body of “highly specialized knowledge” and the “attainment of a bachelor's or higher degree in the specific specialty (or its equivalent) as a minimum for entry into the occupation in the United States.” An alien may be classified as an H-1B specialty occupation worker if the alien possesses “full state licensure to practice in the occupation, if such licensure is required to practice in the occupation,” “completion of [a bachelor's or higher degree in the specific specialty (or its equivalent)],” or “(i) experience in the specialty equivalent to the completion of such degree, and (ii) recognition of expertise in the specialty through progressively responsible positions relating to the specialty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that the bachelor's degree must be in the specific specialty (not “any bachelor's degree”) and that the baseline minimum for eligibility is specialized education or equivalent experienced-based expertise. These aspects influence which subset of OEWS workers should be considered 'similarly employed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline qualification standard for visa categories (H-1B/H-1B1/E-3/EB-2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The INA sets attainment of a bachelor's degree in a specific specialty, or equivalent experience conferring similar expertise, as the baseline minimum for H-1B/H-1B1/E-3; EB-2 requires advanced degrees or exceptional ability above that baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these classifications target workers with higher-than-average qualifications in many occupations, prevailing wage calculations must account for these higher baseline qualifications when identifying comparable U.S. workers and setting wage tiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: OEWS as primary data source for prevailing wages
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department has long relied on OEWS data to establish prevailing wage levels because it is a comprehensive, statistically valid survey covering over 1 million establishments and providing wage levels at national, State, metropolitan, and nonmetropolitan levels and certain territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OEWS wages are straight-time, gross pay and include base rate, cost-of-living allowances, guaranteed pay, hazardous duty pay, incentive pay (commissions and production bonuses), tips, and on-call pay. No commenter identified a more suitable and comprehensive data source than OEWS in the 2021 RFI; however, OEWS is not specifically designed for these visa programs and must be used in a manner that aligns with INA requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of OEWS regarding within-occupation heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: The OEWS survey “captures no information about differences within the [occupational] groupings based on skills, training, experience or responsibility levels of the workers whose wages are being reported.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because INA requires reliance on education, experience, and supervision levels, the Department must account for OEWS's lack of within-occupation differentiation by identifying subsets of workers within OEWS who meet statutory qualification criteria rather than using the entire occupational distribution unadjusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic-area alignment with INA "area of employment"
rubrics_metrics.description: The geographic areas used by BLS to calculate local wages do not always match up exactly with the “area of employment” as defined by the INA for H-1B purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting prevailing wages, the Department must ensure that geographic wage data align with the INA's employment-area definition or otherwise adjust methodology to account for mismatches so that prevailing wages reflect the relevant labor market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of OOH and SOC to identify similarly-employed U.S. workers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department uses the Occupational Outlook Handbook (OOH) and SOC occupational classifications to assess duties and baseline educational requirements for occupations, observing that many OEWS occupational groupings include workers whose education/experience do not match H-1B statutory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis should focus on the subset of workers within SOC categories who possess the same specialized education/experience as visa beneficiaries; OOH entries help indicate whether the ‘typical’ level of education for an occupation aligns with statutory specialty occupation requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discounting lower portion of OEWS distribution for entry-level wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many OEWS occupational classifications include workers who would not qualify for specialty-occupation status, "it would be inappropriate to consider the wages of the least educated and experienced workers in these occupational classifications in setting the prevailing wage levels."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department determined it is appropriate to discount the lower portion of the OEWS distribution when computing entry-level (Level I) wages so that prevailing-wage baselines reflect workers with qualifications comparable to even the least skilled H-1B workers, rather than the entire occupational bottom tail (current Level I uses mean of bottom third and is criticized as too low).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting top-tier (Level IV) wage methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: The current Level IV wage is set by calculating the mean of the upper two-thirds of the OEWS distribution, which can include many workers who do not make more than the median and thus may not possess qualifications commensurate with highest-tier H-1B roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level IV should be revised via statistical modeling to better reflect wages of U.S. workers with the greatest levels of education, experience, and responsibility, restoring labor market fairness and preventing dilution of top-tier wage standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align prevailing wages with education, experience, and supervision levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevailing wage determinations must take into account the experience, education, and level of supervision of occupational classifications so prevailing rates are an appropriate wage floor for positions that require specialized knowledge and skills and/or advanced degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying where in the OEWS distribution workers with comparable specialized education/experience are found allows the Department to adjust wages accordingly; employers may also demonstrate that specific positions require higher qualifications that merit higher prevailing wages (e.g., advanced practice nursing or management roles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply a unified prevailing wage structure across related visa categories to prevent program shopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the same prevailing wage structure across H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, EB-2, and EB-3 helps prevent employers from selecting among visa categories based on wage-setting advantages rather than legitimate labor needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although EB-3 minimum qualifications differ and EB-3 is not the focus of the discounting analysis, the Department applies the same structure to avoid creating incentives for employers to choose visas to exploit lower wage thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise wage floors to mitigate outsourcing/job-shop distortions
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party placement scenarios can undermine the "actual wage" requirement because the H-1B employer of record (outsourcing firm) may compare H-1B pay only to other workers at the outsourcing firm rather than to higher-paid, similarly employed U.S. workers at the end-client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While this rulemaking does not change how actual-wage determinations are applied in third-party placements, raising prevailing wage levels increases the wage floor and reduces pay gaps where outsourcing companies pay at or near prevailing wages, thereby mitigating outsourcing-driven underpayment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evaluation of adverse effects on U.S. worker wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic analysis comparing certified LCAs to OEWS matched by SOC, state, and year showed average wages offered to H-1B workers were approximately $10,191 lower than the OEWS average for similarly classified occupations (larger gaps in computer-related occupations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such empirical findings support recalibrating prevailing wages; the methodology should be informed by administrative data, academic research, and investigations demonstrating that current wage methodology can depress U.S. wages and enable substitution of lower-paid alien labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of labor-supply, degree completions, and technology impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in supply (e.g., rapid growth in domestic degree completions) and demand shocks (e.g., layoffs, generative AI reducing demand for lower-level tech workers) affect the labor market for occupations central to these programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevailing wage methodology must be responsive to labor-market trends so wage levels do not lag current market realities and inadvertently facilitate substitution of alien labor for U.S. workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for telework and geographic labor-market liquidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher telework rates in management, professional, and computer occupations increases the geographical scope of the workplace and contributes to labor market mobility and liquidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because remote work broadens where a worker can be employed, prevailing-wage determinations should account for telework-induced changes in relevant labor markets and possibly the appropriate geographic scope of wage comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent wage arbitrage by ensuring prevailing wage reflects similarly employed U.S. workers
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevailing wage should prevent employers from using alien workers to depress wage levels; wages should be based on U.S. workers similarly employed in education, experience, and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prevailing wages are set too low relative to similarly employed U.S. workers, employers can classify positions at low wage levels and hire lower-paid alien workers, creating systemic cost advantages and undercutting domestic wages and opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow employer demonstration of normal higher qualifications for specific positions
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where an employer seeks a prevailing wage determination for a position that requires higher qualifications than typical for the occupation (e.g., advanced practice or management nursing roles), the prevailing wage determination may reflect the higher requirements, provided the employer demonstrates such requirements are normal for the occupation and the position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits case-specific upward adjustments where employers supply evidence that the position's normal qualifications exceed occupational norms described in sources like the OOH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rigorous statistical/mathematical analysis aligned with statutory mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's proposed methodology is based on substantial economic and administrative data, statistical modeling, and a reasoned policy judgment that the current wage structure does not adequately reflect wages paid to similarly employed U.S. workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodology changes should be justified with rigorous analysis demonstrating how proposed wage-tier calibrations better protect U.S. workers and align with INA objectives; the preamble references modeling and comparison exercises supporting reform.
